newsitem.title: USA: Panel urges privacy protection of health records.
newsitem.headline: Panel urges privacy protection of health records.

text.p: Medical records are vulnerable to invasions of privacy in the computer age but there is not enough public clamour to ensure that safeguards are introduced, an influential health panel said on Wednesday.
"Solutions are available to make electronic records even more secure than paper records," said Paul Clayton, chairman of the National Research Council panel on medical privacy.

"But today there are no strong incentives to safeguard patient information because patients, industry groups, and government regulators aren't demanding protection," said Clayton, of Columbia Presbyterian Medical Centre in New York.

Clayton said solutions could include electronic audits that can trace every access to medical records, backed by tough penalties for violations. In the short term, the panel listed several simple safeguards, such as computer passwords and tighter policies on who needs access to records.
The Department of Health and Human Services must in the next year devise guidelines for protecting computerized records under a health reform bill passed last year.
The panel expressed privacy concerns about one aspect of that law, which calls for "universal patient identifiers" that would provide a nationwide link of all a patient's files.

The panel's report, called "For the Record: Protecting Electronic Health Information," said computerized records can increase accuracy, which can raise the quality of care and cut the costs. But it can also open the door to abuses.
Health information is shared among care-givers -- and among people who do not provide care but who used the information for claim payments or for research.

The panel outlined several steps for health care organisations, including hospitals, insurers and doctors' offices. These steps can be easily enacted, and do not have to wait for the next wave of technology, they said.
People who legitimately need access to information should have computer passwords. Abuses, including leaving the records open at an unattended computer, should be punished.

Organisations should also limit access to the people who genuinely need the information. Remote access should be monitored to make sure outsiders aren't tapping into the system. Special phone lines or encrypted passwords should be considered, and information passed on public networks like the Internet should be coded, the panel said.
Within a few years, there should be better ways to maintain logs of who has looked at records and gotten access to clinical information.
The National Research Council is a private nonprofit institution that provides science and technology advice under a national charter.
